findings.summary: The basics page ends with four code blocks that teach select, for-range over a channel, close, WaitGroup and the fan-in merge goroutine — none of which have been defined yet.
findings.evidence: Page 1 trailing blocks: "select {","case ch <- v: // queued fine","default: // buffer full, drop it"; "for j := range jobs { o <- process(j) }"; "go func(c <-chan T) { // pass c: pre-1.22","\tdefer wg.Done()","\tfor v := range c { out <- v }"; "go func() {","\twg.Wait()  // last producer finished","\tclose(out) // nobody else knows when". `select`/`default` are defined on page 6, `close` and `for range ch` on page 5, and the merge/closer patterns belong to chapters the part never reaches.
findings.fix: Delete these four code blocks from page 1 and restore them to their home sections: the non-blocking send to the select page, the worker body and merge goroutine to the fan-out/fan-in chapters, the `wg.Wait(); close(out)` closer to the closing page.

findings.summary: Page 3's final bullet list begins "Also `qcount`, ...", continuing a list of hchan fields that is only presented on page 4.
findings.evidence: Page 3 last block: ["Also `qcount`, `dataqsiz`, `sendx`, `recvx`","Every operation takes `hchan.lock` first","That is a runtime mutex, not a `sync.Mutex`","Wait queues hold `sudog` records wrapping goroutines"]. The struct those fields belong to first appears on page 4: "type hchan struct {","\tbuf unsafe.Pointer // ring array".
findings.fix: Delete this bullet list from page 3 and place it on page 4 directly under the `hchan` struct code block, replacing "Also" with "Plus" now that `buf`, `sendq`, `recvq` and `lock` precede it.

findings.summary: Every page ends with the next page's opening material, so each titled page starts mid-topic with behaviour rules for something it has not introduced.
findings.evidence: Page 5 ends with "Waiting On Many" (`select { case v := <-a: ... }`) and "default Is Non-Blocking", and page 6 "select: Multiplexing" then opens with "Every case must be a channel operation"; page 6 ends with "The Never-Made Channel" ("var ch chan int // nil, never made"), and page 7 "nil Channels: The Off Switch" opens with "Set the variable to nil once its stream is exhausted".
findings.fix: Shift each spilled tail block onto the page whose title it introduces, so every page opens with its own definition: the two select blocks start page 6, and the nil-channel block starts page 7.

findings.summary: Page 1 closes with the unbuffered-handoff diagram, which uses runtime terms (`sendq`, parking) three pages before hchan is introduced and steals page 2's own conclusion.
findings.evidence: Page 1 final block: diagram nodes ["sender parks","`sendq`","receiver arrives","direct copy","both unparked"]. `sendq` and parking are first explained on page 4 ("`sendq` and `recvq` are wait queues of `sudog` records", "block / `gopark`").
findings.fix: Move this diagram to the end of page 2 (Rendezvous), where the direct handoff has just been described, or to page 4 after `sendq`/`gopark` are named.

findings.summary: The rendezvous page opens by calling `close(done)` a broadcast, using close three pages before closing is taught.
findings.evidence: Page 2 first code block: "done := make(chan struct{}) // 0 bytes","close(done) // wakes every receiver". Close is only defined on page 5 ("`close(ch)` marks it closed; it frees nothing"), where the broadcast property is also stated.
findings.fix: On page 2 show only `done := make(chan struct{})` plus the `done <- struct{}{}` / `<-done` completion signal; drop the `close(done)` line and leave the broadcast claim to page 5.

findings.summary: The buffered-channel introduction (`make(chan int, 3)` and the ring-buffer diagram) sits at the end of the unbuffered page, so page 3 begins with buffer rules for a construct it never introduces.

The diagram also names `hchan` two pages before page 4 defines it.

findings.summary: Both comment lines in the "Semaphore Pattern" code block are cut off at the right edge of the block.

findings.summary: "Values are copied in and copied out again" / "copied twice" is wrong for the direct-handoff path the same page just described, where the value is copied exactly once.
findings.evidence: Bullets: "Values are copied in and copied out again", "A large struct is copied twice, so send a pointer" — directly contradicting the same page's fast-path diagram: "receiver in `recvq`" → "copy to its stack" → "buffer skipped". In `chansend`, a waiting receiver triggers `send()`→`sendDirect()`: one copy, sender stack → receiver stack.
findings.fix: Qualify it: "Through the buffer a value is copied twice (in, then out); on the direct-handoff fast path it is copied once. Either way a large struct is memmove'd — send a pointer."

findings.summary: Three lines in the "The Struct" code block are cut off at the block's right edge, truncating their comments mid-word.
findings.evidence: "buf unsafe.Pointer // ring arr", "sendq, recvq waitq // parked g", "lock mutex // runtime, not syn" — all end at the box border with no closing text
findings.fix: Shorten the trailing comments (e.g. "// ring array", "// parked goroutines", "// runtime lock") or wrap/reflow the code block so full lines fit inside the box width.

findings.summary: The runtime page ends by teaching close semantics — two-value receive, range, and send-on-closed panic — before page 5 defines what close does.
findings.evidence: Page 4 trailing blocks: "v, ok := <-ch // ok=false: closed+drained", "for v := range ch { use(v) } // idiomatic", "A send on a closed channel panics, never errors", and heading "Closer Pattern" with "go func() { wg.Wait(); close(out) }()". Page 5 then opens with the definition: "`close(ch)` marks it closed; it frees nothing".
findings.fix: Move these four blocks to page 5, placing the `v, ok`/range code and the panic bullets after "What close Does" and the closer pattern after the multiple-senders bullets.

findings.summary: The claim that `time.After` leaks its timer until it fires is outdated — since Go 1.23 unreferenced Timers and Tickers are garbage collected immediately, even if never stopped and never fired.
findings.evidence: "`time.After` leaks its timer until it fires" / "In a hot loop use `time.NewTimer` and `defer t.Stop()`" — Go 1.23 release notes: "Timers and Tickers ... are now garbage collected immediately when they become unreachable, even if their Stop methods have not been called. Earlier versions of Go did not collect unstopped Timers until after they had fired."
findings.fix: Rewrite as: "Pre-1.23: `time.After` kept its timer alive until it fired; in a hot loop that piled up. Go 1.23+ collects unreferenced timers immediately, so the leak is gone — `time.NewTimer` + `defer t.Stop()` is still preferred when you need to reset or cancel early."

findings.summary: The busy-spin bug and its fix are demonstrated with bare `select` blocks that contain no enclosing `for`, so the claimed spin and the `continue` statement have no support in the example.
findings.evidence: Page 7 code is "select {","case v, ok := <-a: use(v, ok) // spins","case v, ok := <-b: use(v, ok)","}" yet the bullet claims "After `a` closes, its case fires on every iteration"; the fix block likewise uses "\tif !ok { a = nil; continue } // drop out" with no loop for `continue` to target.
findings.fix: Wrap both code blocks in the loop, e.g. "for a != nil || b != nil {" / "\tselect {" ... "\t}" / "}", so the iteration the spin claim and `continue` depend on is visible.

findings.fix: Change "These ten pages" to "These seven pages".

findings.summary: The caption promises ten pages covering the full channel model, but the part contains seven pages and never reaches fan-out, fan-in or the cheat sheet whose code already appeared on page 1.
findings.evidence: Caption: "These ten pages are the whole channel model"; the deck has 7 slides, ending at "nil Channels: The Off Switch", while page 1 already shows the fan-in merge goroutine ("for v := range c { out <- v }").

findings.summary: `cap(ch)` is fixed at creation and cannot change, so calling it racy alongside `len(ch)` is wrong.
findings.evidence: "`len(ch)` and `cap(ch)` are racy for decisions" / "The value can change before the next line runs" — a channel's capacity is set by `make` and is immutable for the channel's lifetime.
findings.fix: Restrict the claim to `len`: "`len(ch)` is racy for decisions — it can change before the next line runs. (`cap(ch)` is fixed at creation and safe to read.)"

findings.summary: "Every operation takes `hchan.lock` first" is false for the non-blocking (select-with-default) paths, which return without ever acquiring the lock.
findings.evidence: "Every operation takes `hchan.lock` first" — `chansend` begins `if !block && c.closed == 0 && full(c) { return false }` and `chanrecv` has the matching `if !block && empty(c) { ... return }`, both before `lock(&c.lock)`.
findings.fix: Amend to: "Every blocking operation takes `hchan.lock` first; non-blocking select cases have a lock-free early-out."

findings.summary: "`make(chan T, n)` is one block" holds only when the element type contains no pointers; for pointer-bearing element types the runtime makes two allocations.
findings.evidence: "`make(chan T, n)` is one block: header plus `n*sizeof(T)`" — `makechan` only merges when `elem.PtrBytes == 0` (`mallocgc(hchanSize+mem, nil, true)`); the default case is `c = new(hchan); c.buf = mallocgc(mem, elem, true)` — two allocations. Ironically that is the `chan *T` case the next bullet recommends.
findings.fix: Change to: "`make(chan T, n)` is one allocation when `T` has no pointers (header + `n*sizeof(T)` contiguous); with pointer-bearing `T` the header and buffer are allocated separately."

findings.summary: "100k blocked goroutines cost KB" understates the memory by three orders of magnitude — the real figure is hundreds of megabytes.
findings.evidence: "100k blocked goroutines cost KB, not OS threads" — a goroutine's minimum stack is 2 KB plus its `g`/`sudog` bookkeeping, so 100k parked goroutines is roughly 200–400 MB, not kilobytes.
findings.fix: Change to: "100k blocked goroutines cost a few KB each (~hundreds of MB), not 100k OS threads."
